newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan opposition leader shrugs off poll defeat.
newsitem.headline: Japan opposition leader shrugs off poll defeat.

text.p: Japan's top opposition leader Ichiro Ozawa, under fire for a new election defeat, on Monday shrugged off suggestions that he should resign to take responsibility for his party's crumbling strength.

While Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, and at the other end of the political spectrum the Japan Communist Party, celebrated significant gains in Sunday's local Tokyo elections, Ozawa's only answer was that the electorate had failed so far to hear the message of his Shinshinto (New Frontier Party).

The contest for 127 seats in the Tokyo Metropolitan Assembly of 23 inner-city boroughs, suburban municipalities, and rural districts was regarded as a test of voter mood in the country's largest city ahead of national elections next year.
Shinshinto, which held four seats in the old assembly and contested 11 seats, came away empty-handed in the latest sign of its declining strength as a political force.
"We are not interested in the numbers game," Ozawa told reporters. "We will keep the banner high and push forward with our policies on reform."
For Hashimoto, the strong showing by his Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) cleared the political decks for the rest of the year, ensuring his easy re-election as party president in September.

Communist Party parliament member Yasuo Ogata said his party's gains marked a change in Japanese politics which would see the communists become a force in national politics, not just local government, where issues were more parochial.
"There is a new axis in Japanese politics," Ogata said. "Voters want a true opposition such as we are instead of parties that simply try to be an alternative government."
The next national-level elections are due to be held in July 1998 for half of the 252 seats in parliament's Upper House, a less influential chamber than the Lower House.
In the Lower House, the LDP has 245 seats, Shinshinto 139 and the communists 26.

Results announced by the Election Administration Commission showed that in Sunday's poll the LDP won 54 seats to maintain its status as top party in the assembly, up from 38 seats before the election.
The JCP came second with 26 seats, twice its pre-election strength, in the latest strong showing by communists in local government elections.
The number of people eligible to vote in the Tokyo assembly poll numbered 9.4 million, some 10 percent of nationwide electors.
Japanese newspapers said a record low voter turnout of 40 percent showed how low politics had sunk in the public eye.
"The most powerful wind blown was a wind of political distrust, in light of the fact that 60 percent of eligible voters opted not to vote," the Mainichi Shimbun said.
The Nihon Keizai Shimbun said: "The JCP's big advance shows severe criticism of the status quo of politics."
Only hours after the elections results, there was a new blow for Ozawa when his key aide Kazuo Aichi, a former defence minister, quit the party over "policy differences" with his autocratic leader.
Aichi joined former prime ministers Morihiro Hosokawa and Tsutomu Hata in resigning from a party Ozawa formed just two and a half years ago.
LDP officials said their gains also guaranteed stability in a loose coalition with the small Sakigake Party and the Social Democrats, an alliance that allows Hashimoto to govern.
"There is no change in our relation with friendly parties which have adopted common policies. I aim to stabilise national politics," Hashimoto told reporters.
